The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Every $u\in X$ is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz. Define its extended distributional total variation by
$$TV_2(u;\Omega):=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\ \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2),\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}|\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$
where $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ denotes smooth compactly supported vector fields, $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm, and $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\partial_1\varphi_1+\partial_2\varphi_2$. This definition treats $L^2$ functions as almost-everywhere classes and does not require $u\in L^1(\Omega)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.
For every open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the space $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $C_0(\Omega)$ in the uniform norm.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, every bounded real linear functional on $C_0(U;\mathbb R)$ is integration against a unique finite signed Radon measure. No Dependent Choice assumption is required.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$

If $\psi\ne0$, the vector field $\varphi=\psi e_i/\|\psi\|_\infty$ and its negative are admissible in [F1]; hence $|L_i(\psi)|\le M\|\psi\|_\infty$. The same bound is immediate for $\psi=0$. By [F3], $L_i$ extends uniquely to a bounded real linear functional on $C_0(\Omega)$.

Countable Choice and [F4] represent each extension by a finite signed Radon measure $\mu_i$. Formula [F2] identifies $\mu_i$ with $D_i u$, so $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ has finite vector Radon variation by [F5]. For every continuous compactly supported $g$ with $\|g\|_\infty\le1$, approximate uniformly by a smooth compactly supported $h$ with $\|h-g\|_\infty<\varepsilon$, and replace $h$ by $h/\max\{1,\|h\|_\infty\}$. The replacement has norm at most one and differs from $g$ by at most $2\varepsilon$. Since $\sum_i|\mu_i|(\Omega)<\infty$, its integral against $\mu$ approaches that of $g$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Thus the supremum over smooth unit fields equals the continuous-field supremum in [F5]. By [F2], $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi=-\int\varphi\cdot d\mu$; symmetry of the unit test class removes this minus sign. Consequently $|Du|(\Omega)=M=TV_2(u;\Omega)$, proving the assertion.

First suppose $G\subset\mathbb R^2$ is a bounded open set with compact smooth boundary $\Gamma$. The boundary is a compact smooth one-dimensional manifold without boundary. Connected coordinate arcs cover $\Gamma$; compactness gives a finite subcover, so $\Gamma$ has finitely many connected components. By [F5] each component is a smooth embedded circle. Parametrize component $i$ by an orientation-compatible unit-speed smooth periodic curve $\gamma_i:[0,L_i]\to\mathbb R^2$, where $L_i$ is its length. The divergence formula in [F3] gives $D\chi_G=-\nu\,\mathcal H^1|_\Gamma$ with $\nu$ the outward normal, and [F4] therefore gives $P(G;\mathbb R^2)=\mathcal H^1(\Gamma)=\sum_iL_i$. Applying Stokes in [F3] to $\omega=(x\,dy-y\,dx)/2$, whose exterior derivative is $dx\wedge dy$, gives
$$|G|=\frac12\sum_i\int_0^{L_i}(\gamma_{i,1}\gamma'_{i,2}-\gamma_{i,2}\gamma'_{i,1})\,ds.$$
For each $i$, translating $\gamma_i$ by its arclength mean $\bar\gamma_i=L_i^{-1}\int_0^{L_i}\gamma_i(s)\,ds$ does not change this integral, since each coordinate derivative integrates to zero over a period. Write $z_i=\gamma_i-\bar\gamma_i$.

For a smooth $L$-periodic scalar function $z$ of mean zero, set $v(\theta)=z(L\theta/(2\pi))$. Its zeroth Fourier coefficient vanishes. Integration by parts gives $\widehat{v'}(k)=ik\widehat v(k)$ for every integer $k$. Parseval [F6] and $k^2\ge1$ for $k\ne0$ imply $\int_0^{2\pi}|v|^2\,d\theta\le\int_0^{2\pi}|v'|^2\,d\theta$. Changing variables yields
$$\int_0^L|z(s)|^2\,ds\le\left(\frac L{2\pi}\right)^2\int_0^L|z'(s)|^2\,ds.$$
Apply this to both coordinates of $z_i$ and add. Since $|z'_i|=|\gamma'_i|=1$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives
$$\left|\frac12\int_0^{L_i}(z_{i,1}z'_{i,2}-z_{i,2}z'_{i,1})\,ds\right|\le\frac12\|z_i\|_{L^2}\|z'_i\|_{L^2}\le\frac{L_i^2}{4\pi}.$$
Summing over the finitely many boundary components and using $\sum_iL_i^2\le(\sum_iL_i)^2$ proves $4\pi|G|\le P(G;\mathbb R^2)^2$.

Now let $E$ be as in the Statement and put $u=\chi_E$. By [F1], choose $u_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ with $e_j:=\|u_j-\chi_E\|_1\to0$ and $a_j:=\int|\nabla u_j|\to P(E;\mathbb R^2)$. If $|E|=0$, the result is immediate. If some $e_j=0$, continuity forces $u_j$ to take only the values $0$ and $1$ everywhere; connectedness of $\mathbb R^2$ and compact support then force $u_j=0$, contradicting $|E|>0$. Thus $e_j>0$. Let $\tau_j=\sqrt{e_j}$ and discard finitely many terms so $0<\tau_j<\min\{1/2,|E|/2\}$. For every $t\in I_j:=[\tau_j,1-\tau_j]$, a point where $\chi_E$ and $\chi_{\{u_j>t\}}$ differ contributes at least $\tau_j$ to $|u_j-\chi_E|$; hence $|\{u_j>t\}\mathbin\triangle E|\le e_j/\tau_j=\tau_j$.

By [F2], the measurable level-perimeter function has integral at most $a_j$ on $I_j$, whose length is $1-2\tau_j$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, the set of $t\in I_j$ with $P(\{u_j>t\};\mathbb R^2)\le a_j/(1-2\tau_j)+\varepsilon$ has positive measure; otherwise its integral over $I_j$ would exceed $a_j$. The critical values of $u_j$ form a null set by [F2], so choose such a regular value $t_j$ and take $\varepsilon=1/j$. Since $t_j>0$ and $u_j$ is compactly supported, $G_j:=\{u_j>t_j\}$ is bounded and its closure is a compact smooth domain with boundary $\{u_j=t_j\}$. Thus step 1.2 applies to $G_j$, and
$$|G_j\mathbin\triangle E|\le\tau_j,\qquad P(G_j;\mathbb R^2)\le\frac{a_j}{1-2\tau_j}+\frac1j.$$
The right side has limit $P(E;\mathbb R^2)$, while $|G_j|\to|E|$.

Step 1.2 gives $4\pi|G_j|\le P(G_j;\mathbb R^2)^2$ for every selected $j$. Taking upper limits, the convergence $|G_j|\to|E|$ and the perimeter upper bound from step 2.2 give $4\pi|E|\le P(E;\mathbb R^2)^2$. This proves the claimed inequality for every finite-measure finite-perimeter set.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Set $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ for a measure space $(\Sigma,\mu)$, using the real integral inner products; under Countable Choice these are real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $A^*:Y\to X$ be its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$. Define $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ as follows. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

Identify each $q\in X$ with the continuous linear functional $h\mapsto\langle q,h\rangle_X$ by the real Hilbert-space Riesz representation. For exact data $f=Au^\dagger$, a **minimum-TV exact solution** is a point $u^\dagger\in X$ satisfying $Au^\dagger=f$ and $R(u^\dagger)\le R(u)$ for every $u\in X$ with $Au=f$. A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

$$\limsup_{k\to\infty}TV(v_k;\mathbb R^2)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$

$$\int_\varepsilon^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^{-\varepsilon}P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$

If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. On a bounded domain $L^2\subset L^1$, so the relative functional agrees with that test-field functional by [F8]; the Dirichlet version is its composition with the linear isometric zero-extension map into full-space $L^2$. Thus the hypotheses of [F1] hold. Comparison of each objective with its finite value at zero also gives finite TV at a supplied minimizer. Put $z_n=v_{\alpha_n,0}=A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}$. By [F1], $z_n\to v_0=A^*p_0$ strongly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and $v_n=z_n+e_n$ with $\|e_n\|_2\le\eta$. Thus the exact-field sequence, its limit and the noisy fields have precisely the coefficient decomposition required by [F10]. In particular their uniform small-measure moduli and, in full space, exact-field tail moduli follow from strong convergence, as proved there, without an assumed uniform integrability of the noisy perturbations.

For each supplied minimizer, [F1] and positive one-homogeneity imply $R(u_n)=\langle v_n,u_n\rangle$ and $v_n\in\partial R(0)$. The selected TV is even, since its test-field class is symmetric and zero extension is linear. Applying its inequality to both $\chi_F$ and $-\chi_F$ gives $P_*(F)\ge\sigma\int_Fv_n$ for either sign $\sigma$, for every finite-area finite-selected-perimeter competitor; $P_*$ denotes the selected branch perimeter throughout this proof. Indeed these indicators belong to $L^2$ and their selected TV is exactly $P_*$ by [F8] and the boundary conventions. In full space every nonzero level has finite area by $|\{|u_n|>|t|\}|\le\|u_n\|_2^2/t^2$. Bounded-domain levels have finite area automatically. Coarea [F4] gives finite selected perimeter for almost every nonzero level. Relative-perimeter Neumann levels also have finite ambient perimeter by [F11]. Signed layer cake and Cauchy–Schwarz give an absolutely integrable level pairing: the integral over levels of $\int_{E_n(t)}|v_n|$ is $\int|u_n||v_n|\le\|u_n\|_2\|v_n\|_2$. Hence [F11] and coarea show that the integral of the nonnegative gaps $P_*(E_n(t))-\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_{E_n(t)}v_n$ equals $R(u_n)-\langle v_n,u_n\rangle=0$. Each gap therefore vanishes almost everywhere. Their value zero is the global minimum of $P_*(F)-\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_Fv_n$, since every competitor has nonnegative value. This proves the stated equality and even global branch minimization, which in particular implies compact-perturbation variational curvature [F5]. Taking the countable union of exceptional level sets makes this true simultaneously for all $n$.

The threshold and actual obstacle assumptions are exactly those of [F10]. Apply it to every calibrated set from step 1.2, with either level sign. It supplies one $c,r_0>0$ for both ambient density inequalities at every point of each canonical boundary, independently of the index and the nonexceptional level. In the Dirichlet branch the actual obstacle extension uses perimeter submodularity from [F10]; in the Neumann branch its proof uses relative cuts and the specified $C_\Omega$, and at points on $\partial\Omega$ it uses the uniform Lipschitz exterior area for the ambient complement. Thus no false relative-complement estimate is imposed on the valid case $E=\Omega$. In full space [F10] compares $E$ with actual radial cuts and proves finite-radius extinction of $|E\setminus B(0,r)|$, giving one common ball containing the density-one sets and their topological boundaries. Bounded-domain representatives and boundaries lie in $\overline\Omega$. These are the full density and support conclusions, rather than assumptions for the transfer below.

The limiting field calibrates every minimum-TV exact solution $u_0$ under consideration. More explicitly, the dual supplier [F1] defines $p_0\in\{p:A^*p\in\partial R(0),\ \langle f,p\rangle=R(u^\dagger)\}$. For any such exact minimum $Au_0=f$ and $R(u_0)=R(u^\dagger)$, one has $\langle v_0,u_0\rangle=\langle p_0,f\rangle=R(u_0)$, while $v_0\in\partial R(0)$. Its subgradient inequality is therefore also the inequality at $u_0$. Repeat step 1.2 with $u_0,v_0$; its almost-everywhere level sets are calibrated global minimizers. Adjoin the limiting exact field with perturbation zero in [F10]. The very same coefficient moduli and noise threshold used in step 2.1 then give the same uniform density and support conclusions for this limit. This includes any selected minimum-TV exact limit carrying the inherited certificate; it does not identify that solution with $u^\dagger$ without uniqueness.

Fix a nonzero nonexceptional level for which the corresponding sets converge in measure to such a canonical limit $E_0$. If $E_0=\varnothing$ and infinitely many $E_n$ are nonempty, their bounded common support makes each boundary nonempty: a boundaryless subset of connected $\mathbb R^2$ is clopen, and the only bounded clopen set is empty. Choose a boundary point and one fixed $0<r<r_0$; the density estimate gives $|E_n\triangle E_0|\ge c\pi r^2$, a contradiction. If $E_0$ is nonempty, it has positive measure by its density-one definition, so convergence rules out infinitely many empty $E_n$. The empty status therefore agrees eventually; two empty boundaries have Hausdorff distance zero. In the nonempty case, if $x_n\in\partial E_n$ stays at distance at least $\delta>0$ from $\partial E_0$, common compact support and [F9] give a subsequence $x_n\to x$. For $r<\min(r_0,\delta/4)$ the connected ball $B(x_n,r)$ misses $\partial E_0$ and is entirely in $E_0$ or entirely outside it. A fixed smaller connected ball about $y$ misses every corresponding $\partial E_n$, so along a further subsequence its status is always full or always empty. Measure convergence makes $E_0$ full or empty almost everywhere on that ball. By the density-one definition it is then actually full or empty in a smaller ball, contradicting $y\in\partial E_0$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.
Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Every Schwartz function belongs to complex $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, and the classes represented by $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ are dense there.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Every $u\in X$ is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz. Define its extended distributional total variation by
$$TV_2(u;\Omega):=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\ \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2),\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}|\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$
where $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ denotes smooth compactly supported vector fields, $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm, and $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\partial_1\varphi_1+\partial_2\varphi_2$. This definition treats $L^2$ functions as almost-everywhere classes and does not require $u\in L^1(\Omega)$.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $X^*$ be its continuous real dual. The dual pairing is evaluation, written $\langle \xi,x\rangle_{X^*,X}:=\xi(x)$ for $\xi\in X^*$ and $x\in X$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper convex functional: $R$ never takes the value $-\infty$, its effective domain $\operatorname{dom}R:=\{x\in X:R(x)<+\infty\}$ is nonempty, and $R((1-t)x+tz)\le (1-t)R(x)+tR(z)$ for $x,z\in X$ and $t\in[0,1]$, with $0\cdot(+\infty):=0$ for this convex-combination formula. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, its subdifferential is

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Set $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ for a measure space $(\Sigma,\mu)$, using the real integral inner products; under Countable Choice these are real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $A^*:Y\to X$ be its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$. Define $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ as follows. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

Identify each $q\in X$ with the continuous linear functional $h\mapsto\langle q,h\rangle_X$ by the real Hilbert-space Riesz representation. For exact data $f=Au^\dagger$, a **minimum-TV exact solution** is a point $u^\dagger\in X$ satisfying $Au^\dagger=f$ and $R(u^\dagger)\le R(u)$ for every $u\in X$ with $Au=f$. A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.
